title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance (Consolidated ADRs)
author: Avery Chen
content:
Summary:
This consolidated architecture and standards document defines the canonical conventions and minimum requirements for public-facing APIs, application coding, infrastructure-as-code (IaC), model-serving, observability, and performance targets at Redwood Inference. It also references and summarizes the associated Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) that capture trade-offs and long-lived decisions. The goal is to provide a single, maintainable reference for engineers and architects building production-grade inference services.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: Service and platform components owned by Engineering: user-facing APIs (hosted, dedicated, private), backend services, model-serving runtime, infrastructure deployments (cloud and on-prem packaging), and observability/ops artifacts.
- Audience: Backend engineers, infra engineers, runtime engineers, platform owners, SREs, and architects.

Principles (applies across sections):
1. Production-first: prioritize operational safety, observability, and predictable performance over theoretical optimizations.
2. Developer ergonomics: consistent, discoverable patterns reduce onboarding and maintenance cost.
3. Explicit trade-offs: encode trade-offs in ADRs and link to tests and benchmarks.
4. Versioned contracts: APIs, models and infra configs are typed and versioned; backwards-compatibility is managed via documented rollouts.

1) API standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent design of REST/HTTP and internal HTTP/gRPC endpoints used by Redwood services and customers.
Key rules:
- API surface: Use RESTful resource-based routes for public HTTP endpoints; use gRPC for high-throughput internal service-to-service RPCs.
- Naming and versioning: All public endpoints must include a version prefix: /v1/, /v2/. For major breaking changes bump major version. Document deprecation windows and provide migration guides.
- Authentication/Authorization: OAuth2 bearer tokens for hosted API; mTLS + JWT for dedicated/private control-plane signals. Enforce least-privilege RBAC for internal admin endpoints.
- Input validation and schemas: Use OpenAPI v3 for public REST endpoints. All POST/PATCH payloads must include JSON Schema and example payloads in the API spec.
- Error handling: Use structured error responses: {"error": {"code": "ERROR_CODE", "message": "human-friendly message", "details": {...}}}. Error codes must be documented and use 4xx/5xx semantics. Provide stable error codes for common client signals (RATE_LIMITED, MODEL_UNAVAILABLE, INVALID_PROMPT).
- Idempotency: PUT/POST operations with side-effects must support idempotency keys via Idempotency-Key header.
- Rate limiting and throttling: Default tenant-level soft quota of 60 rps for free tier; configurable quotas in Dedicated plans. Signal via RateLimit response headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset).
- Streaming: For streaming responses use Server-Sent Events (SSE) or gRPC streaming. Provide explicit cancelation semantics; clients must be able to signal early termination.
- Contracts and schemas: Publish OpenAPI and protobuf artifacts in the API registry repo with generated SDKs. CI must validate that public API changes include an OpenAPI diff and migration notes.

2) Coding standards
Purpose: Ensure readability, testability, and consistent patterns across codebases.
Language preferences and conventions:
- Primary languages: Go for performance-sensitive services (runtime, infra control), Python for evaluation and higher-level orchestration, TypeScript for web console and SDKs.
- Formatting and linting: Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go; black/ruff/pytest for Python; eslint + prettier for TypeScript. CI must fail on lint/format violations.
- Testing: Minimum test coverage thresholds: 60% for library code, 40% for service entrypoints. All services must include unit tests, and critical paths must have integration tests in CI.
- Dependency management: Use modules (go.mod, pip-tools, pnpm). Avoid transitive dependency surprises by pinning where practical and adding a weekly dependency review.
- Secure coding: Follow OWASP guidance for input handling. All third-party code must be reviewed for licenses and known CVEs; subscribe and respond to vuln alerts within 72 hours.
- Documentation: Every public package must include README with usage examples and exported contract docs.

3) Infrastructure standards (IaC, cloud accounts, network)
Purpose: Standardize provisioning, environment segregation, and secure defaults.
Standards:
- IaC: Terraform is canonical for cloud infra. Module registry lives in infra/terraform-modules. Modules must be small, composable, and documented.
- Environments: Use accounts/projects per environment: dev, staging, prod. Network-level isolation between tenant-facing prod and staging.
- Secrets: Use KMS-backed secret stores (AWS KMS / GCP KMS + Secret Manager). No plain secrets in repos. Automated secret-scanning in CI.
- Networking: Default to private subnets for compute; services that must be public are fronted by load balancers with WAF rules. Use service-managed peering or shared VPC patterns for private deployments.
- RBAC and identity: Prefer short-lived credentials and workload identities (IRSA / Workload Identity). Human access constrained via SSO + SCIM groups.
- CI/CD: All deploys must go through pipeline; manual approvals required for prod changes that touch infra or SLO-affecting code.
- Cost and tagging: Enforce tagging policy (team, service, env, cost-center) at provisioning time. Cost dashboards updated weekly.

4) Model-serving standards
Purpose: Define packaging, rollout, and operational controls for inference models and variants.
Standards:
- Model metadata: Every model in the catalog must include: model_id, semantic_version, architecture, quantization_profile, expected_memory_gb, supported_sequence_lengths, recommended_batching_policy, evaluation_scorecards, and risk notes. Store as versioned YAML metadata in the model-catalog repo.
- Packaging: Containerize model-server entrypoints with immutable image tags referencing both model version and runtime sha. Provide CI checks that verify model artifact integrity (checksum).
- Quantization and performance profiles: Include precomputed quantization artifacts (e.g., int8/4-bit profiles) with validated quality regression thresholds. The quantization profile must include expected token latency delta and bitrate/cost savings.
- Rollouts and canaries: Use canary percentages by traffic with automatic quality checks (prompt-set-based evals) during canary. Canary acceptance gating rules live in the rollout policy document.
- Backwards compatibility: API-level compatibility guaranteed for minor model updates; breaking changes require new model_id or major semantic_version bump. Provide fallback model variants for graceful degradation.
- KV cache and context handling: Runtime must expose configurable KV cache TTLs and provide metrics for cache hit/miss. Document typical cache sizing guidelines per model family.
- Model observability: Export per-model metrics: tokens_generated, inference_latency_p50/p90/p99, cache_hit_rate, batch_size_distribution, queue_time_ms, memory_pressure.

5) Observability standards (logs, metrics, tracing, dashboards)
Purpose: Ensure operators can triage incidents and analyze performance regressions.
Standards:
- Metrics: Use Prometheus-style metrics for infra telemetry. Metric names: service_component_metric (e.g., runtime_inference_latency_ms). Include labels for service, model_id, deployment_env, and route.
- Tracing: Use W3C Trace-Context for distributed traces. Every external request (customer API) must generate a trace that links to model-serving spans.
- Logs: JSON structured logs with stable keys: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, user_tenant, message, err_code. Logs must avoid PII.
- Dashboards & Alerts: Every SLO-bearing service must have a canonical dashboard and alert rules in the observability repo. Alerting noise minimized via aggregation and multi-window checks.
- Retention: Metrics: 90 days for high-cardinality metrics, 24 months for aggregated rollups. Traces: 30 days by default. Logs: 90 days (longer for security audit logs as required).

6) Performance standards and SLOs
Purpose: Define latency and availability expectations and the methods to measure them.
Baseline SLOs (examples):
- Public generation endpoints (hosted API): p50 < 150 ms, p90 < 400 ms, p99 < 1s for short-context (<512 tokens) completion requests. Availability: 99.9% monthly.
- Model-serving internal RPCs (gRPC): p95 < 200 ms under steady-state loads.
- Embeddings endpoints: p90 < 300 ms.
Measurement and testing:
- Synthetic benchmarking: Standard benchmark suite (benchmarking-and-perf-suite) must include per-model and per-sequence-length tests. Bench runs recorded and stored in the perf DB with hardware, model, quantization, and batch size metadata.
- Load testing: Every release that changes batching logic, kernel selection, or scheduling must pass a staged load test that exercises autoscaling policies and burst behavior.
- Cost/perf tradeoffs: Capture token-per-second and $/1000-token numbers in the model catalog to enable routing decisions (smart routing).

7) Decision records (ADRs) and change process
- ADRs: All architectural decisions that materially affect compatibility, security, or SLOs must be captured as ADRs in the architecture-and-standards adr folder. ADRs follow the template: Title, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives considered, Date, Owners.
- Examples summarized:
  - ADR-2025-06: Adopt OpenAPI v3 + generated SDKs for public endpoints (reason: client ergonomics, tooling).
  - ADR-2025-09: Use gRPC for internal high-throughput calls (reason: binary proto perf and contract guarantees).
  - ADR-2026-01: Quantization-first model packaging (reason: consistent perf & cost controls across Dedicated/Private).
- Change review: Changes to these standards require an ADR or an ADR update and a 2-week review cycle with reviewers listed on the top of the document.

8) Ownership, rollout and compliance
- Owners: Each standard area has an owner: API standards (API Guild), Coding standards (Developer Experience), Infra standards (Platform Infra), Model-serving standards (Runtime Team), Observability (SRE), Performance (SRE + Runtime).
- Compliance checks: CI gates and periodic audits (quarterly) to validate adherence. Non-compliance escalated to the owning guild with remediation deadlines.

Appendix A: Quick reference snippets
- Example error response (JSON):
{
  "error": {
    "code": "RATE_LIMITED",
    "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 30s.",
    "details": { "retry_after_seconds": 30 }
  }
}

- Example ADR template (text):
Title: ADR-YYYY-NN - Short description
Context: (problem and constraints)
Decision: (what we decided)
Consequences: (implications and follow-ups)
Alternatives considered: (brief notes)
Date: YYYY-MM-DD
Owners: Team, primary owner

Appendix B: SLO table (examples)
- hosting.gen.completions: availability 99.9%, p90 latency 400ms
- runtime.inference: availability 99.95%, p95 latency 200ms
- embeddings.api: availability 99.9%, p90 latency 300ms

How to contribute / update this doc:
- To propose a change, open an ADR in the architecture-and-standards ADRs folder. If the change is purely editorial and small, submit a PR with the updated doc and tag the reviewers above. All changes must include a rollout/migration plan if they affect compatibility or SLOs.

Related artifacts and repos:
- infra/terraform-modules (repo)
- model-catalog (repo)
- benchmarking-and-perf-suite (repo)
- api-registry (repo with OpenAPI and SDK generation)

Contact / escalation:
For immediate issues that affect production SLOs or security, contact on-call via PagerDuty and follow the oncall-and-incident-response runbooks. For non-urgent clarifications reach out to the owner teams listed above.

This document is intentionally prescriptive where stability and safety are required and intentionally advisory where implementation details may vary (e.g., model-specific batching). For any ambiguous area follow the principle: if in doubt, prefer safety and observability.
